column1: # aes-r3-wind-state.tsv -- AES round 3: what the window manager remembers
# between calls.
# Format (seven tab separated columns):
#   opcode  n_intin  n_intout  n_addrin  n_addrout  intin values  comment
# as cases/aes-r1.tsv, cases/aes-r2-wind.tsv and cases/aes-r2b-rlist.tsv,
# and read by the same loader (core/cases.c).  A '+' opcode is a PRELUDE:
# issued after the reset and before the measured call, never recorded.  A
# case id is the PHYSICAL LINE NUMBER and this file's CRC binds every dump
# to it, so ANY edit -- an appended case, a fixed typo in a comment --
# invalidates every dump already taken with it.  This file is written once;
# a later question goes into a later table, never into this one.
# THE FOUR QUESTIONS THIS TABLE ANSWERS
# Each of the four is settled in the EmuTOS source and unsettled on real
# hardware: the two frozen tables that could have asked -- aes-r2-wind.tsv
# (CRC AFB11C9F) and aes-r2b-rlist.tsv (CRC B4CC4A5A) -- have no case for
# any of them and may not be given one, because their CRCs carry the dumps
# already taken.  Hence a new table rather than four new cases.
# A. WHO OWNS THE SEARCH POINTER of WF_FIRSTXYWH / WF_NEXTXYWH?  In EmuTOS
#    it belongs to the window: ORECT *w_rnext is a field of WINDOW
#    (aes/gemlib.h:85), picked out by pwin = get_pwin(w_handle) before the
#    walk (aes/gemwmlib.c:1513, :1559) and written in exactly one place,
#    w_owns (:1235).  So FIRST(1), FIRST(2), NEXT(1) has to answer window
#    1's SECOND piece: the FIRST on the other window cannot have moved
#    window 1's pointer.  An implementation holding ONE pointer for the
#    whole AES answers the end of window 2's list instead.  This is not an
#    exotic order -- two GEM programs redrawing at the same time produce
#    exactly this interleaving, and so does one program with two windows.
#    Section A.
# B. WHAT DO THE THREE WINDOW RECTANGLES SAY AFTER wind_close?  wm_close
#    does not close by clearing a flag.  It calls draw_change(w_handle,
#    &gl_rzero) (aes/gemwmlib.c:1449, :1453) and drops VF_ISOPEN only
#    afterwards (:1454), and draw_change writes WS_PREV = the old WS_CURR
#    (:1069-1070), WS_CURR = the rectangle handed in (:1073) and WS_WORK =
#    wm_calc(WC_WORK, kind, that rectangle) (:1074-1077) -- all three
#    BEFORE the "this window isn't open, we're done" shortcut
#    (:1084-1085).  After a close, therefore: WF_CXYWH is 0,0,0,0
#    (gl_rzero, aes/gemgraf.c:425), WF_PXYWH is the rectangle the window
#    had, and WF_WXYWH is the work area of a ZERO rectangle, which for a
#    window with borders has negative w and h.  The two early returns
#    (:1444-1447) are the other half of the contract: a window that was
#    never open must come back untouched, and that is what protects the
#    desktop window, VF_INUSE but never VF_ISOPEN.  Section B measures each
#    of the three fields on its own call, before and after, plus the
#    machine's own wind_calc answer to compare WF_WXYWH against.
# C. WHICH OF THE FOUR WORDS DOES THE END OF THE LIST WRITE?  w_owns has
#    TWO ends (aes/gemwmlib.c:1230-1241), and they do not write the same
#    number of words:
#        while (po) {
#            rc_copy(&po->o_gr, poutwds);
#            pwin->w_rnext = po = po->o_link;
#            if (rc_intersect(pt, poutwds))
#                return;
#        poutwds->g_w = poutwds->g_h = 0;
#    P1, the loop is never entered: :1240 writes g_w and g_h and nothing
#    else.  P2, the loop runs but no piece survives the clip: all four
#    words are written, because rc_intersect assigns its four components
#    even when it returns FALSE (util/rectfunc.c:63-78 -- the four
#    assignments at :72-75 stand before the return at :77), so g_x and g_y
#    are those of the LAST piece examined.  aes-r2b-rlist.tsv reached P1
#    three times and P2 never: it has no case in which a window's list is
#    non-empty and yet nothing in it meets the work area.  Section C builds
#    exactly that, and pairs it with the P1 that follows one call later, so
#    both ends stand in one dump.
# D. WHAT DOES A THIRD WINDOW DO TO THE DECOMPOSITION?  A window's list is
#    rebuilt by newrect (aes/gemwrect.c:165-205), which starts from its own
#    WS_TRUE rectangle and lets every later window break it: w_obadd adds a
#    newly opened window as the LAST child of the root (gemwmlib.c:186-202)
#    and newrect's everyobj walk stops at the window being opened
#    (gemwrect.c:198, everyobj's this == last test at gemobjop.c:93), so a
#    window's list is broken by the windows opened AFTER it, in the order
#    they were opened.  brkrct then cuts every SURVIVING piece again
#    (gemwrect.c:101-132, pieces in the fixed order TOP, LEFT, RIGHT,
#    BOTTOM, :30-33), so the order in which the two covering windows arrive
#    decides how many pieces there are and where the cuts fall -- the
#    visible AREA is the same either way, the decomposition is not.  Two
#    windows can never show this; aes-r2b-rlist.tsv opens two.  Section D
#    walks the same bottom window's list under the same three rectangles
#    twice, differing only in the order the two upper windows were opened.
# NOT HERE, deliberately: the appl_init re-entry gap.  Its read path is
# closed -- appl_read blocks on an empty queue (core/cases.c's opcode
# guard, gemaplib.c:88), and empty is precisely the failing case -- so it
# needs a measurement design of its own, not a case in this table.
# THE ONE RULE, UNCHANGED: NEXT IS NEVER MEASURED WITHOUT A FIRST BEFORE IT
# w_setup (aes/gemwmlib.c:205-228) initialises w_owner, w_flags, w_kind,
# w_pname, w_pinfo and the four slider fields.  It does NOT initialise
# w_rnext, and w_rnext is written in exactly one place in the whole AES:
# w_owns (:1235).  On a freshly created window it therefore still holds
# whatever the slot's previous life left -- an ORECT pointer newrect has
# since handed back to the free list (gemwrect.c:174-181).  A measured
# WF_NEXTXYWH with no WF_FIRSTXYWH before it would dereference that and
# follow its o_link, which is not merely unreproducible but unsafe on a
# machine nobody is watching.  Every NEXT in this file -- measured OR
# prelude -- carries a FIRST on the SAME handle earlier in the same case.
# The interleaved cases of section A satisfy it per handle, not per case:
# the NEXT(2) cases carry a FIRST(2), the NEXT(1) cases a FIRST(1).
# Section B is the one place where a window is closed, and it contains no
# FIRST and no NEXT at all.  That is on purpose: ob_delete takes the window
# out of the tree before draw_change rebuilds the lists (gemwmlib.c:1452
# against gemwrect.c's newrect), so a NEXT carried across a close would
# walk a list nobody owns any more.  That is a question with no answer in
# the source, and this table does not ask it.
# WHAT THE POISON MAKES VISIBLE HERE
# The runner poisons int_in, int_out, addr_in and addr_out with 0xDEAD
# before every call, measured and prelude alike (core/runner_aes.c).  In
# this table it carries three separate pieces of information:
#   1. THAT NOTHING WAS WRITTEN PAST OUT_LEN.  Every wind_get case here
#      declares OUT_LEN 5 and the AES record holds seven int_out words, so
#      int_out[5] and int_out[6] must come back 0xDEAD on both machines.  A
#      value there is a dispatcher writing past what the caller declared,
#      not a window-manager answer.
#   2. THAT NOTHING WAS WRITTEN BACK INTO THE INPUTS.  int_in beyond the
#      values a case lists, and both address arrays, stay poisoned: the
#      dispatcher copies control, int_in and addr_in onto local buffers and
#      never writes them back (aes/gemsuper.c:435-439).
#   3. IT DOES *NOT* SEPARATE P1 FROM P2 BY ITSELF, and section C does not
#      ask it to.  xif copies OUT_LEN words back out of a local int_out it
#      never initialised (aes/gemsuper.c:432, copy-back :444-445), so on a
#      P1 end the caller's poisoned x and y are overwritten with whatever
#      that stack buffer held -- not poison, and not reproducible.  A15 has
#      already traced the 31/63 and 0/19 the TT returned there to the
#      caller's own history.  What separates the two ends is therefore the
#      CONTENT of x and y in the P2 case, which is predicted from the
#      geometry, against the P1 case measured in the same run.
# SAFETY
# Every rule core/cases.c enforces holds here unchanged, and this file
# stays inside the limits the two round 2 tables proved on both machines:
#   * six opcodes appear, all of them with a NULL refusal in aes_opcodes[]:
#     wind_create (100), wind_open (101), wind_close (102), wind_get (104),
#     wind_set (105), wind_calc (108).  Nothing blocks on the operator,
#     nothing ends or replaces the application, nothing is gated out of TOS
#   * three distinct handles are ever opened -- 1, 2 and 3 -- against the
#     loader's bound of four.  Each open sends the dumper one WM_REDRAW it
#     never reads; doq unions them per handle (gemqueue.c:45-56), so three
#     of the queue's eight slots are the worst case.
#   * no wind_open(0), no wind_delete at all, no wind_set on handle 0, no
#     wind_update and therefore no unpaired END_MCTRL, and no wind_get or
#     wind_set field that carries a pointer (WF_NAME, WF_INFO, WF_NEWDESK)
#     or an unchecked array index (WF_COLOR, WF_DCOLOR).
#   * every rectangle that reaches the screen is non-negative and lies
#     inside 640x400 including its drop shadow, so nothing is clipped on
#     one machine and not on the other.  The largest is 180,160,200,160,
#     whose WS_TRUE corner is 382,322.
#   * the one call that could outlive its own case -- wind_close(0), which
#     would matter only on a machine that wrongly wrote the desktop's
#     rectangle, since wm_new sweeps handles >= 1 only (gemwmlib.c:1886) --
#     is the LAST case in the file, so even that outcome cannot reach
#     another case.
# The run draws: windows open, move and close on screen, exactly as the
# round 2 runs did.  wind_get, wind_calc and wind_close write no pixels of
# their own.
# WHAT IS DEVICE DEPENDENT, AND WHY THE CASES STILL COMPARE
# Every rectangle answer carries the border arithmetic of wm_calc, which
# runs on gl_wbox / gl_hbox -- font metrics, and a device parameter, the
# same one round 1 measured through wind_calc.  Two devices are in play:
# the TT at 640x480 and the Pi at 1920x1080.
# The cases are built so that what DECIDES each question does not depend on
# those metrics:
#   * section A decides on whether a NEXT answers a piece or an end --
#     w and h non-zero against w and h zero.
#   * section B decides on gl_rzero (a constant, gemgraf.c:425), on a
#     rectangle this table itself set, and -- for WF_WXYWH -- on the
#     machine's OWN wind_calc(WC_WORK, 0x0FEF, 0,0,0,0), which is measured
#     here as a case so the comparison is made per machine.
#   * section C's two pieces lie outside window 1's own rectangle entirely
#     when the drop shadow is applied, and on its last two border pixel
#     columns and rows when it is not; either way they are border and not
#     work area on any machine whose right and bottom borders are two
#     pixels or more, which a window with a sizer and both sliders always
#     has.  The work area is measured as its own case so the precondition
#     can be checked on the machine rather than assumed.
#   * section D decides on how many pieces there are and in which order,
#     and on whether the two groups differ from each other AT ALL -- a
#     comparison inside one machine's own run.
# The absolute coordinates are recorded, not compared away.
# opcode\tn_intin\tn_intout\tn_addrin\tn_addrout\tintin\tcomment

column1: # B. The three window rectangles across a wind_close
# The window is opened at 30,40,320,240 and then MOVED to 70,90,260,180
# with wind_set(WF_CXYWH) before it is closed.  The move is what gives the
# section its edge: wm_open overwrites WS_PREV with the opening rectangle
# afterwards (gemwmlib.c:1427), so without a later move WF_PXYWH would read
# the same before and after the close and could not tell an implementation
# that writes the three fields from one that writes nothing at all.
# Each field is asked on its own call.  WF_FXYWH is asked too, as the
# control: wm_close has no business touching it -- WS_FULL has exactly
# three writers, wm_create, wm_delete and wm_init (gemwmlib.c:1380,
# :1479, :1293), and none of them is on this path.

column1: # C. A list that is not empty and still meets nothing: the P2 end
# Window 2 sits on the SAME top left corner as window 1 and is two pixels
# shorter in width and in height.  Two consequences, and the case needs
# both:
#   * have_piece[TOP] and have_piece[LEFT] are false (gemwrect.c:113-114),
#     so what is left of window 1 is a RIGHT piece and a BOTTOM piece and
#     nothing else -- the list is NOT empty, which is what P1 would be.
#   * both pieces are two pixels wide or high and sit on window 1's outer
#     edge: with the drop shadow applied they lie outside window 1's own
#     rectangle altogether, without it on its last two border rows and
#     columns.  Either way they are border, never work area, so every
#     rc_intersect in the walk fails and the walk runs to the end.
# What must then arrive: ret = 1, w = h = 0 from gemwmlib.c:1240, and x and
# y WRITTEN -- those of the last piece examined after rc_intersect has
# clamped them to the work area, i.e. x = max(BOTTOM piece x, work x) and
# y = window 1's y + window 2's h + the drop shadow.  Four written words,
# not two.  The work area and both current rectangles are measured here as
# their own cases so that this can be recomputed on each machine instead of
# being assumed.

column1: # D. Three windows, and the order they were opened in
# The same three rectangles in both groups -- 1 at 30,40,320,240, 2 over
# its top left at 60,80,200,160, 3 over its bottom right at 180,160,200,160
# so that 3 overlaps both 1 and 2 -- and the same window walked, window 1.
# The ONLY difference between the two groups is the order 2 and 3 were
# opened in, and therefore the order in which they broke window 1's list.
# Group I opens 1, 2, 3: the list is broken by 2 and then by 3.
# Group II opens 1, 3, 2: the list is broken by 3 and then by 2.
# The visible area is identical in both.  The decomposition is not: brkrct
# cuts each surviving piece again, so under this geometry the source
# predicts four pieces for group I and five for group II, with different
# cuts.  Nobody has to trust those two numbers for the section to decide
# something, and that is the point of running both: an implementation that
# subtracts the covering rectangles in HANDLE order instead of in the order
# they were opened cannot tell the two groups apart and must answer the
# same in both.  Group I is also where the middle window is asked -- window
# 2 is broken by 3 while itself breaking 1, which two windows cannot show.

column1: # E. The desktop window, and why it is last
# D.w_win[0] is VF_INUSE from wm_init on but never VF_ISOPEN, so wm_close
# must turn round at gemwmlib.c:1446-1447 and leave its rectangle alone.
# If a machine wrote it anyway, WS_CURR would become gl_rzero and every hit
# test on the desktop would lose its screen -- and wm_new sweeps handles
# >= 1 only (:1886), so no reset in this run would undo it.  That is the
# one outcome in this file that could reach another case, which is why this
# case is the last line of the table.
